title: EY Published a Cybersecurity Report. Sixty Per Cent of Its Citations Were Made Up by AI.
excerpt: The Big Four firm pulled its ‘Points of Attack’ report after researchers found most of its references were fabricated or unverifiable — a case study in what happens when AI-generated content slips past editorial review at the world’s most trusted consultancies.
body:
Ernst & Young Canada published a cybersecurity report called ‘Points of Attack’ that examined fraud vulnerabilities in loyalty and rewards systems. It was the kind of polished, data-heavy document that Big Four firms produce by the hundreds — the kind that lands in boardrooms, shapes procurement decisions, and gets cited in regulatory filings. There was one problem: roughly 60 per cent of its citations were fabricated.

## How It Unravelled

The unravelling began when independent researchers ran the report’s bibliography through verification tools, including GPTZero, a platform designed to detect AI-generated content. What they found was damning. More than half the cited sources either did not exist, pointed to papers with different titles and authors, or referenced journals that had never published the work attributed to them. The hallmarks were textbook AI hallucination: plausible-sounding author names, realistic journal formatting, and DOIs that led nowhere.

EY Canada withdrew the report and issued a statement confirming it was “reviewing its publication process.” The firm did not specify which AI tools had been used in the report’s preparation, nor did it clarify how the document cleared EY’s internal quality assurance. The report has since been scrubbed from EY’s public-facing research portal.

## A Systemic Problem, Not an Isolated Incident

EY’s embarrassment arrives against a backdrop of mounting evidence that AI-generated citations have become a systemic problem across professional and academic publishing. A 2026 Columbia University study identified roughly 4,000 fabricated references in 2,800 published research papers — a figure the authors called “almost certainly an undercount.” A separate analysis in The Lancet found that one in every 277 academic papers now contains at least one AI-hallucinated citation.

The consulting industry, which relies on speed and volume of output, is particularly vulnerable. Analysts and associates at firms like EY, Deloitte, McKinsey, and PwC routinely use generative AI tools to draft research sections, compile literature reviews, and source supporting data. The efficiency gains are real — a task that once took a junior analyst three days can now be completed in an afternoon. But the verification step, the boring, unglamorous work of checking whether a cited paper actually says what you claim it says, has not kept pace.

## The Trust Premium

For the Big Four, credibility is the product. Clients do not pay EY ₹50 lakh for a cybersecurity assessment because the analysis is necessarily better than what a boutique firm could produce; they pay for the EY imprimatur — the assurance that the work has been vetted, reviewed, and stress-tested against the firm’s global knowledge base. When that imprimatur is attached to fabricated citations, the damage extends far beyond one report.

The incident has already prompted the International Federation of Accountants to call for industry-wide guidelines on AI use in professional services publishing. Several large consulting firms have reportedly begun requiring manual citation verification as a mandatory step before external publication — a process some partners have privately described as “a step backward” in productivity.

## India’s Stake in the Conversation

Indian-origin professionals make up a significant share of the Big Four’s global workforce, from entry-level analysts in Bengaluru and Hyderabad to partners in New York and London. The AI tools that generated EY’s phantom citations are, in many cases, built and maintained by Indian engineers at major AI labs. The irony is pointed: the same talent pool that is building these systems is now being asked to clean up after them.

For Indian IT services companies — TCS, Infosys, Wipro — the EY episode is both a warning and an opportunity. As enterprises demand more rigorous AI governance, the market for verification, auditing, and responsible-AI consulting is growing. Indian firms that can position themselves as the trustworthy layer between raw AI output and boardroom-ready deliverables stand to capture a significant share of that market.

The deeper question, though, is cultural. Generative AI rewards speed and fluency. Professional consulting rewards accuracy and trust. The EY report is a reminder that the two do not always coexist — and that in the race to ship faster, even the world’s most meticulous firms can lose sight of what they are actually selling.
